savings-goal-calculator.assumptionNote: Assumes monthly deposits at month-end, constant interest compounded monthly, and that you never withdraw. Taxes and inflation are not included.
benefits: Turns a scary big goal into a concrete monthly number you can act on today.
Shows exactly how much interest shortens the journey - free money for waiting.
Makes trade-offs visible: save $100 more a month and see the years melt away.

faqs.a: Roughly 3 to 6 months of essential expenses is the standard emergency-fund target. Big one-off goals - a house down payment, a car, a wedding - are usually 10 to 30% of the purchase price. Pick a number, enter it, and the calculator does the rest.
faqs.q: How do I choose a savings goal?

faqs.a: Use the interest rate your account actually pays. If you do not know it, 4% is a reasonable placeholder for a decent savings account in 2026. The time difference between 1% and 5% on a 10-year goal is often 1 to 2 years.
faqs.q: What interest rate should I enter?

faqs.a: Only if the goal is years away. Compounding needs time to matter: over 2 years, interest barely moves the needle. Over 10+ years it can shave off many months of deposits. Either way, a higher rate never hurts.
faqs.q: Does the interest rate matter much?

faqs.a: Then this formula cannot give you a finish date - you would never reach the goal. Enter the smallest amount you can truly commit to; even $50 a month reaches $50,000 in about 83 years at 0%, which is honest math telling you to raise the deposit or shrink the goal.
faqs.q: What if I cannot deposit anything monthly?

faqs.a: Two levers: raise the monthly deposit, or raise the rate by moving the money to a higher-yield account. A third option people forget: shrink the goal. A $40,000 goal reached is infinitely better than a $50,000 goal abandoned.
faqs.q: How can I reach my goal faster?

faqs.a: Enter your goal amount and the date you need it by, then solve backwards: divide the goal by the number of months. A $24,000 goal in 4 years needs $500 a month before interest. Use this calculator to refine the number with interest included.
faqs.q: How do I save for a goal with a deadline?

savings-goal-calculator.formula:
With interest: months n = ln((goal x r + PMT) / PMT) / ln(1 + r), where r is the monthly rate and PMT the monthly deposit.
Without interest: months = goal / PMT.
Years = floor(months / 12), leftover months = months - years x 12.
howTo: Enter your target amount - the full price of whatever you are saving for.
Enter how much you can deposit every month, honestly.
Enter the annual interest rate your savings will earn.
Read how many years and months it will take, plus how much interest contributes.
Adjust the monthly deposit until the timeline fits your plans.
keyFacts: Time to goal comes from solving the annuity formula backwards for n.
With interest: n = ln((goal x r + PMT) / PMT) / ln(1 + r).
Without interest it is simple division: months = goal / monthly deposit.
Interest earned is largest near the end, when the balance is biggest.
Doubling the deposit roughly halves the time; raising the rate helps less than raising the deposit.

savings-goal-calculator.quickAnswer: To find how long saving takes, solve the compound-interest formula backwards: with monthly deposits PMT at monthly rate r, months = ln((goal x r + PMT) / PMT) / ln(1 + r). For example, saving $400 a month at 4% toward a $50,000 goal takes about 104.7 months - 8 years and 9 months. You deposit about $41,864 and interest contributes roughly $8,136. Bump the deposit to $500 and the wait drops to about 7 years and 5 months.
savings-goal-calculator.tagline: Find out exactly how long it takes to reach your savings goal.
savings-goal-calculator.workedExample:
Goal $50,000, $400/month, 4% annual:
1. Monthly rate r = 0.04 / 12 = 0.003333.
2. Months n = ln((50,000 x 0.003333 + 400) / 400) / ln(1.003333).
3. = ln(566.67 / 400) / ln(1.003333) = ln(1.41667) / 0.003328.
4. = 0.34831 / 0.003328 = 104.66 months.
5. That is 8 full years plus 8.66 months - about 8 years and 9 months.
6. Deposits = 400 x 104.66 = about $41,864; interest covers the remaining ~$8,136.
